_note: Quote of the day (/savoirs/citations). French-language quotations only, in their traditional wording with modern spelling, by authors who died before 1946, which puts them in the public domain under life+70 in France (Saint-Exupéry, who died in 1944, and other authors with a ‘mort pour la France’ extension are left out on purpose, because their works are still protected in France). Every quote is a line from the author's own work and `source` names that work; `year` is the year of first publication or performance or, for a text that circulated in manuscript or as a letter, of writing or first printing. Lines known to be misattributed are left out on purpose (for example Madame Bovary, c'est moi; Je ne suis pas d'accord avec ce que vous dites…, wrongly given to Voltaire; Ouvrir une école, c'est fermer une prison, wrongly given to Hugo).Verse line breaks are ' / ' (oneLine() in zitateData.js turns them into spaces). `disputed: true` would show a badge; no quote needs it. `meaning` says the quote in plain English (A2–B1). Word fields keep their old names: `de` is the French word, `art` is le, la, l' or les (only for nouns; where it is l' the hint says masculine or feminine), `pos` for other words. Written 2026-11-12. Wording and years were reviewed against what we know of the works, not against an edition; see the to-verify list in the culture report.

moliere.name: Molière
moliere.bio: Molière, whose real name was Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was an actor, the head of a theatre company and the author of comedies such as Tartuffe and L'Avare. He made fun of greedy, proud and false people. His plays are still performed all the time in France, and French is sometimes called “the language of Molière”.
moliere.kurz: He wrote comedies about greedy and proud people.

lafontaine.name: Jean de La Fontaine
lafontaine.bio: La Fontaine put old animal stories into elegant verse. His Fables, published from 1668, are still learned by heart by many French children. Behind the animals he describes the habits of people at court and in town.
lafontaine.kurz: He wrote fables in which animals speak.

montaigne.name: Michel de Montaigne
montaigne.bio: Montaigne was a lawyer and for some years the mayor of Bordeaux. Later he retired to a tower on his estate and wrote his Essais, in which he looks at himself and at life with honest curiosity. He made the word “essay” the name of a type of writing.
montaigne.kurz: He wrote the first famous essays.

pascal.name: Blaise Pascal
pascal.bio: Pascal was a gifted scientist: as a young man he built one of the first calculating machines. Later he turned to religion and wrote short, sharp thoughts on human life, collected after his death as the Pensées. The unit of pressure, the pascal, is named after him.
pascal.kurz: A scientist who also wrote the Pensées.

voltaire.name: Voltaire
voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, wrote plays, stories, letters and essays. He fought for tolerance and against injustice, and he often had to leave France because of what he wrote. His short novel Candide is still widely read.
voltaire.kurz: He wrote Candide and fought for tolerance.

rousseau.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
rousseau.bio: Rousseau was born in Geneva and lived much of his life in France. He wrote about politics, education and about his own life, for example in Du contrat social and Les Confessions. His ideas about freedom and the people influenced the French Revolution.
rousseau.kurz: He wrote about freedom and society.

hugo.name: Victor Hugo
hugo.bio: Hugo wrote Notre-Dame de Paris and Les Misérables, and many poems. He was against Napoléon III and lived in exile on the islands of Jersey and Guernsey for nearly twenty years. When he died, a huge crowd followed his coffin to the Panthéon in Paris.

baudelaire.name: Charles Baudelaire
baudelaire.bio: Baudelaire wrote Les Fleurs du mal, a book of poems about the beauty and the sadness of city life. After it appeared in 1857 he was taken to court for offending public morals. Today he is seen as one of the founders of modern poetry.
baudelaire.kurz: A poet of the modern city.

rimbaud.name: Arthur Rimbaud
rimbaud.bio: Rimbaud wrote nearly all his poems as a teenager and gave up writing before he was twenty-one. After that he travelled and worked in Africa as a trader. He died young, at thirty-seven, but his work still has a very strong influence.
rimbaud.kurz: A teenage poet who stopped writing at 20.

flaubert.name: Gustave Flaubert
flaubert.bio: Flaubert wrote very slowly and looked for the exact word in every sentence. His novel Madame Bovary (1857) brought him to court, but he was not found guilty. It is often seen as a model of the modern novel.

zola.name: Émile Zola
zola.bio: Zola wrote the Rougon-Macquart, a series of twenty novels about one family in the time of the Second Empire. In 1898 he published an open letter, J'accuse…!, in which he defended Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer who had been wrongly condemned. He was convicted and had to leave France for a time.

verlaine.name: Paul Verlaine
verlaine.bio: Verlaine wrote poems that sound like music. His life was difficult: he was a friend of Rimbaud, shot him in the hand in Brussels in 1873 and went to prison. In 1944 the first lines of his poem Chanson d'automne were used on the radio as a secret message to the French Resistance before the landings.
verlaine.kurz: A poet whose verses sound like music.

apollinaire.name: Guillaume Apollinaire
apollinaire.bio: Apollinaire was born in Rome to a Polish mother and lived in Paris, where he was a friend of many painters. His book Alcools (1913) brought new forms to French poetry, for example poems without punctuation. He was wounded in the First World War and died of influenza in 1918.
apollinaire.kurz: A poet of Paris and of modern art.

proust.name: Marcel Proust
proust.bio: Proust spent his last years mostly in his bedroom, writing À la recherche du temps perdu, a very long novel about memory and time. In its best-known scene a taste of tea and a small cake, the madeleine, brings back his childhood.
proust.kurz: He wrote a long novel about memory.

balzac.name: Honoré de Balzac
balzac.bio: Balzac planned a huge series of novels, La Comédie humaine, to describe French society of his time. The same characters return in many of the books. He worked at night and drank a lot of coffee.
balzac.kurz: He described French society in dozens of novels.

stendhal.name: Stendhal
stendhal.bio: Stendhal is the pen name of Henri Beyle. He served under Napoléon, lived in Italy for many years and wrote Le Rouge et le Noir (1830) and La Chartreuse de Parme (1839). He had few readers in his lifetime, but today he is one of the great names of French literature.
stendhal.kurz: He wrote Le Rouge et le Noir.

descartes.name: René Descartes
descartes.bio: Descartes lived many years in the Netherlands and wrote his main works in Latin and French. He wanted to start from doubt and find what is certain. He died in Stockholm, where he had been invited by Queen Christina of Sweden.
descartes.kurz: A philosopher who started from doubt.

larochefoucauld.name: François de La Rochefoucauld
larochefoucauld.bio: La Rochefoucauld was a duke who took part in the political troubles of his youth. Later he wrote the Maximes, short sentences that say that people often act out of self-love, even when they seem generous. Many are still quoted today.
larochefoucauld.kurz: He wrote short, sharp sentences about human nature.

rabelais.name: François Rabelais
rabelais.bio: Rabelais was a monk and later a doctor. He wrote funny, strong and sometimes rude stories about the giants Pantagruel and Gargantua. He also loved to invent and play with words, and he had a big influence on French literature.
rabelais.kurz: He wrote funny stories about giants.

dubellay.name: Joachim du Bellay
dubellay.bio: Du Bellay belonged to the group of poets called La Pléiade. In 1549 he wrote a text that defended the French language as a language for great poetry. He spent some years in Rome, and there he wrote Les Regrets, sad and sometimes funny sonnets about missing home.
dubellay.kurz: A Renaissance poet who missed his home.

ronsard.name: Pierre de Ronsard
ronsard.bio: Ronsard was the best-known poet of La Pléiade and was called the “prince of poets” in his time. He wrote odes, sonnets and love poems with many images from nature. Many French people still know his poem about the rose by heart.
ronsard.kurz: A Renaissance poet of love and roses.

corneille.name: Pierre Corneille
corneille.bio: Corneille wrote tragedies about honour, duty and love. His play Le Cid (1637) was a huge success, and also caused a famous quarrel among writers. With Molière and Racine he is one of the three big names of French theatre of the 17th century.

musset.name: Alfred de Musset
musset.bio: Musset was a poet of the Romantic age. He wrote lively plays, for example On ne badine pas avec l'amour, and sad, personal poems. For some time he had a love affair with the writer George Sand.

lamartine.name: Alphonse de Lamartine
lamartine.bio: Lamartine became famous with his first poems, the Méditations poétiques (1820), which are about love, nature and loss. Later he went into politics, and in 1848 he was part of the government after the revolution of February.
lamartine.kurz: A Romantic poet who became a politician.

beaumarchais.name: Pierre-Augustin Caron de Beaumarchais
beaumarchais.bio: Beaumarchais was the son of a watchmaker and worked as a musician, a businessman and a secret agent before he became a famous playwright. His comedies Le Barbier de Séville and Le Mariage de Figaro made fun of the privileges of the nobility. Operas by Rossini and Mozart are based on them.

quotes.author: moliere
quotes.text: Il faut manger pour vivre, et non pas vivre pour manger.
quotes.meaning: We eat to stay alive. We should not live only to eat. In the play the miser Harpagon hears this said to him.

words.hint: to eat
to be alive; to live
for; in order to

quotes.author: moliere
quotes.text: Que diable allait-il faire dans cette galère ?
quotes.source: Les Fourberies de Scapin, act II
quotes.meaning: What on earth was he doing in that mess? People still say it when someone has got into trouble that he could have avoided.

words.hint: an old rowing ship; today also a difficult, unpleasant situation
the devil; used for emphasis, like ‘on earth’
to do; to make

quotes.author: moliere
quotes.text: Par ma foi ! il y a plus de quarante ans que je dis de la prose sans que j'en susse rien.
quotes.meaning: Monsieur Jourdain learns that everything he says that is not poetry is called prose. He is surprised: he has spoken prose for forty years without knowing it. ‘Susse’ is an old, literary form of ‘savoir’.

words.hint: ordinary writing or speech, not poetry
faith; ‘par ma foi’ = honestly, really
without; it is followed by the subjunctive

quotes.author: lafontaine
quotes.text: La raison du plus fort est toujours la meilleure.
quotes.source: Le Loup et l'Agneau (Fables, book I)
quotes.meaning: In the fable the wolf wants to eat the lamb and finds reasons for it. The strongest always finds a way to be right.

words.hint: a reason; here: an argument
strong; ‘le plus fort’ is the strongest
always

quotes.author: lafontaine
quotes.text: Rien ne sert de courir ; il faut partir à point.
quotes.source: Le Lièvre et la Tortue (Fables, book VI)
quotes.meaning: Running is of no use. You must start at the right moment. In the fable the slow tortoise wins the race because the hare thinks he has time.

words.hint: to run
to leave; to set off
at the right time

quotes.author: lafontaine
quotes.text: Patience et longueur de temps / Font plus que force ni que rage.
quotes.source: Le Lion et le Rat (Fables, book II)
quotes.meaning: Patience and a long time do more than strength or anger. In the fable a small mouse frees the lion from a net by slowly biting the ropes.

words.hint: the ability to wait calmly
how long something is; ‘longueur de temps’ = a long time
strong, wild anger

quotes.author: lafontaine
quotes.text: Tout flatteur vit aux dépens de celui qui l'écoute.
quotes.source: Le Corbeau et le Renard (Fables, book I)
quotes.meaning: Anyone who flatters you lives at your cost. The fox praises the crow's voice so that the crow drops its cheese.

words.hint: a person who says nice things to get something
always plural; ‘aux dépens de’ = at the expense of
to listen to

quotes.author: montaigne
quotes.text: Que sais-je ?
quotes.meaning: What do I know? This was Montaigne's motto. He means that we know much less than we think.

words.hint: to know a fact; je sais, tu sais
what (in a question)
I; ‘sais-je’ puts ‘je’ after the verb in a question

quotes.author: montaigne
quotes.text: Si on me presse de dire pourquoi je l'aimais, je sens que cela ne se peut exprimer qu'en répondant : parce que c'était lui, parce que c'était moi.
quotes.meaning: Montaigne is writing about his friend Étienne de La Boétie, who died young. If you push me to say why I loved him, I can only answer: because it was him, because it was me.

words.hint: to push; to press someone to do something
to say or show in words
to answer

quotes.author: pascal
quotes.text: Le cœur a ses raisons que la raison ne connaît point.
quotes.meaning: Our feelings have reasons that logic does not know. The Pensées were printed after Pascal's death.

words.hint: the heart; also what we feel
reason, logic; also a cause
an older, stronger way to say ‘ne … pas’

quotes.author: pascal
quotes.text: L'homme n'est qu'un roseau, le plus faible de la nature ; mais c'est un roseau pensant.
quotes.meaning: A person is only a reed, the weakest thing in nature, but a reed that can think. Pascal says that thinking is what makes people great.

words.hint: a thin plant that grows by water and bends in the wind
not strong; the same for masculine and feminine
from ‘penser’; a thinking person or thing

quotes.author: pascal
quotes.text: Tout le malheur des hommes vient d'une seule chose, qui est de ne savoir pas demeurer en repos dans une chambre.
quotes.meaning: All the unhappiness of people comes from one thing: they cannot stay quietly in a room. We look for noise and activity so that we do not have to think about ourselves.

words.hint: great unhappiness; bad luck
rest, quiet; the plural looks the same
to stay, to remain (formal)

quotes.author: voltaire
quotes.text: Il faut cultiver notre jardin.
quotes.meaning: We must look after our own garden. After many troubles Candide stops arguing about big questions and decides to work on what is near him.

words.hint: a garden
to grow plants; also to develop something
our (before a singular noun); plural: nos

quotes.author: voltaire
quotes.text: Le mieux est l'ennemi du bien.
quotes.meaning: Trying to make something perfect can spoil what is already good. In the verse Voltaire says that a wise Italian wrote this.

words.hint: better; as a noun, ‘le mieux’ is the best
masculine: l'ennemi (une ennemie for a woman)
what is good; in the plural, property

quotes.author: rousseau
quotes.text: L'homme est né libre, et partout il est dans les fers.
quotes.source: Du contrat social, book I, chapter 1
quotes.meaning: People are born free, but everywhere they live in chains. These are the first words of Rousseau's book on politics.

words.hint: masculine: l'homme; a man, or people in general
free; the same for masculine and feminine
iron; ‘les fers’ is an old word for chains

quotes.author: hugo
quotes.text: Ceux qui vivent, ce sont ceux qui luttent.
quotes.meaning: Those who really live are those who fight. Hugo wrote these poems against Napoléon III while he was in exile.

words.hint: to fight; to struggle
to live

quotes.author: hugo
quotes.text: Demain, dès l'aube, à l'heure où blanchit la campagne, / Je partirai.
quotes.meaning: Tomorrow, at first light, when the fields turn pale, I will leave. The poet will walk all day to visit the grave of his daughter, who died young.

words.hint: feminine: l'aube; the first light before sunrise
the countryside; fields
to become white or pale

quotes.author: baudelaire
quotes.text: Là, tout n'est qu'ordre et beauté, / Luxe, calme et volupté.
quotes.source: L'Invitation au voyage (Les Fleurs du mal)
quotes.meaning: There, everything is order and beauty, luxury, calm and pleasure. The poet invites someone he loves to a dream country.

quotes.author: baudelaire
quotes.text: Il faut être toujours ivre. Tout est là ; c'est l'unique question.
quotes.meaning: You must always be drunk. That is all there is to it. The poet says you can be drunk on wine, on poetry or on goodness, so that you do not feel the weight of time.

words.hint: drunk; the same for masculine and feminine

quotes.author: baudelaire
quotes.text: Homme libre, toujours tu chériras la mer !
quotes.source: L'Homme et la mer (Les Fleurs du mal)
quotes.meaning: Free man, you will always love the sea! The sea is like a mirror of the human soul, wide and never at rest.

words.hint: the sea; feminine
to love dearly (literary)
masculine: l'homme

quotes.author: rimbaud
quotes.text: Je est un autre.
quotes.source: Lettre à Paul Demeny (lettre du voyant)
quotes.meaning: I is somebody else. When Rimbaud writes, he feels that another person speaks inside him. The strange grammar, ‘Je est’ instead of ‘Je suis’, is on purpose.

quotes.author: rimbaud
quotes.text: Il faut être absolument moderne.
quotes.meaning: You must be completely modern. Rimbaud says that you must not look back and that you have to live in your own time.

words.hint: ‘il faut’ means ‘it is necessary’ or ‘you must’

quotes.author: flaubert
quotes.text: La parole humaine est comme un chaudron fêlé où nous battons des mélodies à faire danser les ours, quand on voudrait attendrir les étoiles.
quotes.meaning: Human words are like a cracked pot on which we beat tunes for dancing bears, while we want to touch the stars. We cannot say our deepest feelings in words.

to touch someone's feelings; to make tender

quotes.author: zola
quotes.text: La vérité est en marche, et rien ne l'arrêtera.

quotes.author: verlaine
quotes.text: Il pleure dans mon cœur / Comme il pleut sur la ville
quotes.meaning: My heart is crying as it rains on the town. The poet compares his sadness to the rain.

words.hint: to cry, to weep
to rain; only ‘il pleut’

quotes.author: verlaine
quotes.text: Les sanglots longs / Des violons / De l'automne / Blessent mon cœur / D'une langueur / Monotone.
quotes.meaning: The long sobs of the autumn violins hurt my heart with a slow, dull sadness. The sound of the violins is like crying.

words.hint: a sound you make when you cry hard

a soft, sad tiredness

quotes.author: apollinaire
quotes.text: Sous le pont Mirabeau coule la Seine / Et nos amours / Faut-il qu'il m'en souvienne / La joie venait toujours après la peine
quotes.meaning: The river Seine flows under the Mirabeau bridge, and so do our love and the time we had together. Joy always came after sorrow. The poet remembers a lost love.

quotes.author: proust
quotes.text: Les vrais paradis sont les paradis qu'on a perdus.
quotes.source: Le Temps retrouvé (À la recherche du temps perdu)
quotes.meaning: The real paradises are the ones we have lost. We see the value of happy times only when they are over and we remember them.

quotes.author: proust
quotes.text: Le seul véritable voyage, le seul bain de Jouvence, ce ne serait pas d'aller vers de nouveaux paysages, mais d'avoir d'autres yeux.

quotes.author: balzac
quotes.text: À nous deux maintenant !
quotes.meaning: Now it is between the two of us! These are the last words of the novel. The young Rastignac looks at Paris from a hill and challenges the city.

quotes.author: stendhal
quotes.text: La beauté n'est que la promesse du bonheur.
quotes.meaning: Beauty is only the promise of happiness. We like beautiful things and people because they seem to promise something good.

quotes.author: descartes
quotes.text: Je pense, donc je suis.
quotes.source: Discours de la méthode, part IV
quotes.meaning: I think, so I exist. Descartes doubted everything, but he could not doubt that he was thinking. This was his first certain truth.

quotes.author: descartes
